name: Expert System
definition: A program that captures the knowledge of human experts as facts and IF–THEN rules and uses an inference engine to reach conclusions about a narrow topic.
example: A help-desk system that diagnoses a printer fault from the lights a user reports.

name: Decision Support System (DSS)
definition: An information system that combines data, a model and an interface to help people make decisions, without making them alone.
example: A supermarket tool that forecasts demand and suggests next week's order for a manager to adjust.

name: Unstructured Decision
definition: In NESA's framing, a decision with no complete set of instructions, so human judgement is required.
example: Deciding whether a start-up should open a second shop in another town.

name: Semi-structured Decision
definition: A decision made with a specified set of finite instructions, where a person may still review or approve the result.
example: A loan officer approving an exception to a risk score calculated by fixed rules.

name: Structured Decision
definition: A decision that is fully specified and can be automated, so the system decides and acts without intervention.
example: A warehouse system reordering an item when stock falls below a set level.

name: Knowledge Base
definition: The part of an expert system that stores facts and IF–THEN rules about a specific topic.
example: The eight watering and sun-stress rules in a plant-care advisor.

name: Inference Engine
definition: The part of an expert system that applies the rules in the knowledge base to the known facts to reach conclusions.
example: An engine that fires a rule to add overwatered to working memory, then fires the next rule.

name: Forward Chaining
definition: An inference technique that evaluates existing data with the rules to develop new data and reach a decision.
example: Starting from leaves_yellow and soil_wet, an engine adds overwatered and then reduce_watering.

name: Backward Chaining
definition: An inference technique that starts from a goal and tracks back through the rules to establish the facts and steps needed to prove it.
example: To prove repot_with_drainage, the engine checks root_rot_risk, then overwatered, then the observed facts.

name: Explanation Facility
definition: A feature of an expert system that shows why a question was asked or how a conclusion was reached, usually by displaying the rules used.
example: A tree showing that reduce_watering came from rule R5, which used overwatered, which came from rule R1.

name: Certainty Factor (CF)
definition: A number, here from 0 to 1, that shows how strongly a piece of evidence or a rule is believed.
example: A rule with CF 0.8 and evidence with CF 0.7 gives a conclusion with CF 0.56.

name: Fuzzy Logic
definition: Reasoning with degrees of truth between 0 and 1 instead of only true or false.
example: A temperature of 24 degrees is Warm to degree 0.6 and Hot to degree 0.4.

name: Truth Maintenance
definition: A technique that records the reasons for each conclusion so it can be withdrawn automatically when its supporting facts change.
example: Retracting overwatered when the user corrects soil_wet to dry.

name: Hypothetical Reasoning
definition: A technique that follows the consequences of an assumption in a separate context, then adopts or discards it.
example: A roster system assuming a nurse works Thursday night and rejecting the option after a rest-period clash.

name: Heuristic
definition: An experience-based rule of thumb that finds a good-enough answer quickly without guaranteeing the best one.
example: A mechanic's rule to check the battery first.

name: Ontology
definition: A formal description of the concepts in a domain and the relationships between them, used to classify items and infer inherited properties.
example: A product ontology in which trail running shoe is a kind of running shoe, which is a kind of footwear.

name: Webometrics
definition: The quantitative study of web resources, including the links between pages, their content and how they are used.
example: Analysing which sites link to a page to estimate how relevant it is.

name: Intelligent Agent
definition: A program that senses its environment, decides and acts to achieve a goal, from simple rule-following agents to complex learning agents.
example: A web crawler that follows links (simple) and a ranking system that learns from clicks (complex).

name: Predictive Search String
definition: A suggested completion of a search query, chosen by estimating what the user is most likely to type.
example: Typing how to cook and being offered how to cook rice.

name: Actuator
definition: A device that converts a control signal into a physical action, such as opening a valve or switching a relay.
example: A vent actuator that opens when a greenhouse is too hot.

name: Generative AI
definition: Artificial intelligence that produces new content, such as text, images, audio or code, from patterns learned in very large datasets.
example: A chatbot that drafts a summary of a meeting from a transcript.

name: Digital Twin
definition: A virtual copy of a physical machine, building or process that is updated with live sensor data and used to test changes and predict faults.
example: A model of a pump that shows when its vibration pattern suggests a failure.

name: Surplus Data
definition: Data that is duplicated, unused, out of range or beyond the purpose of the system, and so adds cost and risk without adding value.
example: A probe reading every second when only 15-minute averages and alerts are needed.

name: Mean Absolute Error
definition: The average size of the differences between proposed and actual values, ignoring whether they are above or below.
example: Absolute errors of 75 units over eight weeks give a mean absolute error of about 9.4 units.
